title: Psalms for the sick
hookLine: communities divide the whole book to read for someone who is ill
last: SOW IN TEARS, REAP IN JOY.

lines: THE WHOLE BOOK, FOR ONE PERSON.
cards: The news comes into the group chat late at night. Someone's mother is in the hospital. It's serious.
Within an hour, something happens that's become common in Jewish communities: a list appears. Psalms one to ten, Sarah. Eleven to twenty, David.
Twenty-one to thirty, the Cohens. By the next evening, a whole community of people, some of whom have never met the sick woman, has read the entire Book of Psalms for her.

teach.b: Saying psalms for someone who is ill is a custom kept in many Jewish communities. When there's nothing else to do, this is something to do.
Often it's shared: a group divides all one hundred fifty psalms, so the whole book gets said for one person, sometimes every day.
The person is named the Hebrew way, with their own name and their mother's: Sarah, daughter of Rachel.
Some add a custom with Psalm one nineteen, the long psalm arranged by the Hebrew alphabet: they read the sections whose letters spell the sick person's name. Some psalms are often chosen.
Psalm twenty: "The LORD answer thee in the day of trouble". Psalm thirty, the song of someone who cried out and was healed. And the prayer for healing goes back to the Torah.
When Moses' sister Miriam became ill, Moses cried out five short Hebrew words: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee." No long speech. Just her, and now.
Jews also say a prayer called Mi she-berakh for the sick when the Torah is read, and wish each other refuah shlemah, a complete healing, of body and spirit.
The psalms don't replace doctors; Jewish tradition values medicine deeply. The Talmud teaches that visiting the sick is itself a kind of healing.
But when you're far away, or the waiting room has gone quiet, or there's nothing left to try, a psalm is something you can hold, together.

how: Jewish communities organize Tehillim groups that divide the Book of Psalms for someone who is ill, name them in the Mi she-berakh prayer at the Torah reading, and wish them refuah shlemah.

o: nothing. there's nothing to do from far away.
divide the Book of Psalms and read it for her.

practice: Think of someone who is sick right now, in body or in spirit, picture their face, and say their name quietly.
If you can, find Psalm twenty or Psalm thirty and read it for them; if not, use Moses' five words, heal her now, or heal him now, or just hold them in your mind with a wish for a complete healing.
If you pray, pray for them in your own words.
